premises.text: The Court recorded a fifty-year lease of the land to the Mimanis commencing on 1 January 1939, without a renewal clause, ending on 31 December 1988.
premises.time_scope: 1 January 1939–31 December 1988
premises.speaker: Supreme Court (Banerjee J., judgment)
premises.stage: Supreme Court civil appeal following requisition release
premises.quote: without any clause for renewal and thus the lease expired on 3 1 .12. 1 988 by efflux of time.
limitations: Recorded by the target court; not independent examination of the lease instrument.

premises.text: The Court recorded that the State took possession of the land under requisition on 25 November 1987, before the term of the lease expired.
premises.time_scope: 25 November 1987
premises.speaker: Supreme Court (Banerjee J., judgment)
premises.stage: Supreme Court civil appeal following requisition release
premises.quote: The possession of the land admittedly in terms of the order of requisition was taken on 25th November, 1987
limitations: The target judgment calls this admitted; it is not an independently authenticated possession record.

premises.text: The Court characterized requisition as a temporary transfer of physical control to the State without displacing the owners' ownership, absent acquisition.
premises.time_scope: From November 1987 during requisition
premises.speaker: Supreme Court (Banerjee J., judgment)
premises.stage: Supreme Court civil appeal following requisition release
premises.quote: ownership of the property remains with the owners even during the time the requisition continues.
limitations: The quoted proposition qualifies the requisition in the target case; acquisition is treated as a separate possibility, not an established event.

premises.text: The first High Court appellate judgment, after addressing expiry of the requisition statute, directed restoration to the owner and/or occupier as appropriate and granted liberty to mention difficulties.
premises.speaker: Calcutta High Court appellate bench (as reported)
premises.stage: High Court appellate/release proceedings
premises.quote: the owner and/or the occupier, as the case may be, within 7 days from the date of the Judgment
limitations: The disjunctive wording did not itself identify which competing claimant should receive the property; the Supreme Court did not decide the statutory-lapse issue afresh.

premises.text: Following the first High Court judgment, the Collector notified the Mimanis' advocate of an intended handover on 4 June 1997.
premises.time_scope: 28 May–4 June 1997
premises.speaker: Supreme Court narrating Collector correspondence
premises.stage: Supreme Court civil appeal following requisition release
premises.quote: informed the Advocate for the Mimanis to remain present at the site to receive back the possession
limitations: A proposed administrative handover is not proof of the former lessees' entitlement or of actual delivery.

premises.text: The owners' advocates opposed delivery to the Mimanis, claiming that they were neither owners nor occupiers and requesting delivery to the owners.
premises.time_scope: 29 May and 2 June 1997
premises.speaker: Advocates for Daw-family owners
premises.stage: High Court appellate/release proceedings
premises.quote: the Mimanis were otherwise not entitled to receive the possession as they were neither the owners not the occupiers of the property.
limitations: TRUE means the objection was recorded, not that its underlying legal conclusion was independently proved.

premises.text: The Collector reported competing restoration claims and suspended the proposed delivery while awaiting High Court clarification or other clear direction.
premises.time_scope: After the letters of 29 May and 2 June 1997
premises.speaker: Collector of Howrah (quoted note)
premises.court_level: Administrative correspondence reported in Supreme Court
premises.stage: High Court appellate/release proceedings
premises.quote: the programme of delivery of possession which was communicated to him by the memo under reference is kept in abeyance
limitations: This is the judgment's quotation of the Collector's account; it does not establish actual physical handover.

premises.text: On the owners' later application the High Court made a further order directing possession to the owners, while preserving parties' rights and the former lessees' opportunity to pursue separate proceedings.
premises.time_scope: After 21 May 1997, before the notice of 17 June 1997
premises.speaker: Calcutta High Court appellate bench (as reported)
premises.stage: High Court appellate/release proceedings
premises.quote: directs making over of possession to the owners without prejudice to the rights and contentions of the parties
limitations: Distinct from the first judgment; a direction to deliver possession is not proof delivery occurred.

premises.text: Gupta argued that a person from whom property was requisitioned should ordinarily be the person to whom the State returns it.
premises.time_scope: Supreme Court appeal argument, exact date unspecified
premises.speaker: Dipankar Gupta for the Mimanis
premises.stage: Supreme Court civil appeal following requisition release
premises.quote: if possession has been taken from a particular person the same ought to be allowed to be received back by that particular person and none other.
limitations: Argument for a general principle, not a target-court finding that it controls this expired-lease case.

premises.text: Gupta also objected that the second High Court decision reopened the first judgment, which he characterized as finally deciding restoration to the owner and/or occupier.
premises.time_scope: Supreme Court appeal argument, exact date unspecified
premises.speaker: Dipankar Gupta for the Mimanis
premises.stage: Supreme Court civil appeal following requisition release
premises.quote: connotes final disposal and denotes specifically the determination of the issue raised in the matter.
limitations: His identification of the Mimanis as the proper occupiers remained contested; his procedural objection was assessed separately.

premises.text: The Supreme Court agreed that liberty to mention or apply could not be used to reopen a signed final judgment and considered the second High Court judgment unwarranted on that procedural footing.
premises.time_scope: Supreme Court examination of the successive High Court judgments
premises.speaker: Supreme Court (Banerjee J., judgment)
premises.stage: Supreme Court civil appeal following requisition release
premises.quote: strictly speaking in the contextual facts, the second judgment of the High Court is not warranted by reason of the specific direction as contained in the first judgment.
limitations: Procedural criticism must not be misreported as a determination that the former lessees were entitled to delivery.

premises.text: Despite the procedural criticism, the Supreme Court elected to examine possession entitlement under Article 136 because of extensive merits argument and elapsed time.
premises.time_scope: Supreme Court appeal, judgment 23 July 2001
premises.speaker: Supreme Court (Banerjee J., judgment)
premises.stage: Supreme Court civil appeal following requisition release
premises.quote: the matter has been argued at length on merits before this Court
limitations: The citation is to the Court's choice to adjudicate the merits, not a free-standing finding of automatic restoration.

premises.text: Counsel for the respondents submitted that delivery to the Mimanis required a current right to possession, which the expired lease without a renewal clause did not supply.
premises.time_scope: Supreme Court appeal argument, exact date unspecified
premises.speaker: Advocates for the respondents
premises.stage: Supreme Court civil appeal following requisition release
premises.quote: the Mimanis will have to have some right to obtain the possession
limitations: Attributed submission, not an independently proved source of title.

premises.text: Gupta invoked section 7(3) of the 1948 statute concerning compensation to interested persons, arguing that expiry of the lease did not extinguish all the lessees' interest in the land.
premises.time_scope: Supreme Court appeal argument, exact date unspecified
premises.speaker: Dipankar Gupta for the Mimanis
premises.stage: Supreme Court civil appeal following requisition release
premises.quote: the factum of being disinterested in the land so far as the lessees are concerned after expiry of the lease does not and cannot arise.
limitations: A claim concerning compensation or continuing interest is not itself an adjudicated right to be restored to possession.

premises.text: Venugopal argued from section 6 that the State should inquire into the person presently entitled to possession rather than automatically return land to the erstwhile lessee.
premises.time_scope: Supreme Court appeal argument, exact date unspecified
premises.speaker: Mr. Venugopal for the respondents
premises.stage: Supreme Court civil appeal following requisition release
premises.quote: incumbent upon the State Government to make an inquiry and ascertain the factum of entitlement to possession
limitations: An advocate's reading of the expired statute, not an independently operative statutory duty in this proceeding.

premises.text: The Supreme Court reasoned that the temporary requisition statute had expired and its provisions could not be invoked as operative law for this dispute.
premises.time_scope: At Supreme Court assessment after lapse of the statute
premises.speaker: Supreme Court (Banerjee J., judgment)
premises.stage: Supreme Court civil appeal following requisition release
premises.quote: none of the provisions can be invoked.
limitations: The Court separately discussed the former section 6 conditionally; do not convert that hypothetical reading into an operative statutory basis.

premises.text: The Supreme Court added that even if the lapsed statute's intention were considered, section 6 contemplated inquiry into current entitlement because circumstances and the eligible recipient could change.
premises.time_scope: Hypothetical construction during Supreme Court review
premises.speaker: Supreme Court (Banerjee J., judgment)
premises.stage: Supreme Court civil appeal following requisition release
premises.quote: the situation may change and the entitlement may also change
limitations: Expressly hypothetical, since the Court had already held that the lapsed statute's provisions could not be invoked.

premises.text: The Supreme Court reproduced a lessee letter to the Chief Minister acknowledging that the lease had no renewal clause and had not been renewed.
premises.time_scope: Letter prior to lease expiry; precise date not supplied
premises.speaker: Lessee writing to the Chief Minister (as quoted by the Supreme Court)
premises.court_level: Correspondence described in Supreme Court judgment
premises.stage: Supreme Court civil appeal following requisition release
premises.quote: There is no renewal clause in the said lease, and the same has not been renewed
limitations: The letter is quoted by the judgment; its authenticity, date, and signing individual are not independently supplied.

premises.text: The Supreme Court treated the Mimanis as already out of possession under requisition when the lease expired, unlike an expired lessee continuing physically in possession.
premises.time_scope: From State takeover in 1987 through expiry in 1988 and restoration stage in 1997
premises.speaker: Supreme Court (Banerjee J., judgment)
premises.stage: Supreme Court civil appeal following requisition release
premises.quote: Mimanis stands, admittedly dispossessed from the lease premises.
limitations: The distinction is based on possession held by the State; no owner-instigated forcible eviction is found.

premises.text: The Supreme Court acknowledged the rule that an expired lessee actually remaining in possession retains juridical protection against eviction without due process.
premises.time_scope: Legal comparison stated during Supreme Court appeal
premises.speaker: Supreme Court (Banerjee J., judgment)
premises.stage: Supreme Court civil appeal following requisition release
premises.quote: a person who is in possession or a tenant, whose lease had expired but not having been evicted in accordance with the law has legal protected and possessory right
limitations: This is the acknowledged general proposition; it does not establish that the Mimanis remained in possession, nor equate juridical and lawful possession.

premises.text: The Supreme Court held the continuing-occupant protection inapposite because the Mimanis had lost possession to the State during the lease term and sought restoration only after its expiry.
premises.time_scope: Requisition interval and post-expiry request for restoration
premises.speaker: Supreme Court (Banerjee J., judgment)
premises.stage: Supreme Court civil appeal following requisition release
premises.quote: The lessee has lost his possessory right and the same stands shifted on to the State
limitations: The quote concerns this court's account of legal possessory control, not an adjudication against all independent rights or a general permission for forcible dispossession.

premises.text: The Supreme Court rejected treating the out-of-possession Mimanis as tenants holding over or tenants at sufferance: both comparisons depended on retained possession after lease expiry.
premises.time_scope: After 31 December 1988
premises.speaker: Supreme Court (Banerjee J., judgment)
premises.stage: Supreme Court civil appeal following requisition release
premises.quote: Are the Mimanis in possession? The answer again can not, but be in the negative.
limitations: The Court distinguished possession with and without lessor assent; it did not find that they remained on the land under either status.

premises.text: The later High Court judgment reasoned that the Mimanis could receive no appellate relief after their lease interest ended, and distinguished this from a forcible taking by the owners.
premises.time_scope: Second High Court judgment after May 1997
premises.speaker: Calcutta High Court appellate bench (quoted in Supreme Court)
premises.stage: High Court appellate/release proceedings
premises.quote: it is not a case that the lessor or the owner had forcibly taken over possession.
limitations: This lower-court reasoning is separately attributed; the Supreme Court criticized parts of the later High Court judgment.

premises.text: The Supreme Court recognized that Gupta's criticism of quoted remarks in the later High Court decision was justified, while proceeding to merits review rather than treating the objection as resolving entitlement.
premises.time_scope: Supreme Court review of second High Court judgment
premises.speaker: Supreme Court (Banerjee J., judgment)
premises.stage: Supreme Court civil appeal following requisition release
premises.quote: and we also do feel justifiably so
limitations: The criticism is of the lower court's observations and procedural handling, not the whole of the target court's substantive reasoning.

premises.text: The Court recorded that Mohan Lal Mimani brought a specific-performance suit alleging an oral contract with the owners to purchase the property.
premises.time_scope: Suit instituted by the 2001 judgment; precise allegation date not supplied
premises.speaker: Mohan Lal Mimani, as reported by Supreme Court
premises.court_level: Collateral suit as reported in Supreme Court judgment
premises.stage: Supreme Court civil appeal following requisition release
premises.quote: on the basis of an allegation that there was an oral agreement between the Mimanis and the owners for sale of the property.
limitations: TRUE establishes that the allegation was made, not that an oral sale agreement existed or was enforceable.

premises.text: The Supreme Court recorded that the specific-performance suit had been dismissed for default, with an application for restoration filed but no ruling on that application shown.
premises.time_scope: As described in the Supreme Court judgment of 23 July 2001
premises.speaker: Supreme Court summarizing collateral proceeding
premises.stage: Supreme Court civil appeal following requisition release
premises.quote: an application for restoration has been filed, the records depict no order has been passed thereon and the same is still pending.
limitations: Do not infer ultimate disposition of the application or merits of the claimed oral agreement.

premises.text: The Supreme Court expressly preserved the High Court's reservation of the parties' rights to pursue a recovery action or enforcement of a purchase agreement in independent proceedings according to law.
premises.time_scope: Supreme Court judgment of 23 July 2001
premises.speaker: Supreme Court (Banerjee J., judgment)
premises.stage: Supreme Court civil appeal following requisition release
premises.quote: we do also feel it convenient to record such a reservation of right.
limitations: A reservation of procedural opportunity is not proof the separate claims will succeed; the final disposition is not used as evidence for this premise.

relations.reason: The defined expiry date, together with the State takeover, fixes the lease termination while the former lessees were out of possession.
The documented transfer to the State grounds the target court's finding that the Mimanis were not continuing occupants.
The State's temporary control explains absence of the lessees' possession without treating the owners as actual takers.
The Collector's proposed Mimanis handover prompted the owners' competing claim; the communications evidence disagreement, not two completed transfers.
The owners' objection was one of the competing claims leading the Collector to suspend delivery.
The stalemate over the first order led to the owners' further application and later High Court order.
The first order left open owner and/or occupier; the later order specified owners, an additional order subsequently criticized as procedurally unwarranted.
The general return-to-original-possessor argument was rejected on the distinct facts of State possession and expiration of the lease.
The Court substantially accepted the objection that liberty to mention could not reopen final issues.
The target court criticized the procedural authority for the later High Court order without deeming that criticism dispositive of entitlement.
Procedural criticism and independent Article 136 merits examination coexisted; neither was treated as negating the other.
The respondents' insistence on current entitlement matched the Court's case-specific distinction, but counsel's argument is not itself proof.
The former lessees' reliance on a provision of the temporary Act faced the Court's refusal to invoke its expired provisions.
The Court considered the respondents' inquiry construction only conditionally after refusing direct invocation of the lapsed Act.
The hypothetical interpretation of section 6 was not a revival of the expired provision.
The judgment's quotation of the lessee letter corroborates its finding of no renewal clause and no renewal, subject to documentary limits.
The lack of continued possession defeats both holding-over and sufferance analogies on these facts.
The Court accepted the due-process protection of a continuing occupant yet treated that general principle as inapplicable to these already out-of-possession lessees.
The Court's factual finding that State possession displaced the lessees explains why continuing-occupant protection did not yield restoration.
Rejection of holding-over or sufferance characterizations reinforced the distinction from a lessee still in possession.
The Supreme Court found criticism of quoted lower-court reasoning justified; lower findings must not be collapsed into target-court holdings.
Despite criticizing the later High Court's observations, the Supreme Court considered merits after extensive argument.
The procedural history of the suit establishes neither the truth nor final rejection on the merits of the alleged oral purchase agreement.
An unresolved collateral procedural route remains separate from the Court's reservation of independent remedies.
Denial of restoration through this requisition proceeding did not adjudicate separately reserved causes of action.

coverage_limits: This is a historical reconstruction of case 840688 and the two registered requests under a research-translation registry, not universal law, legal approval, or a human gold annotation.

All factual premises and quoted documents are attributed to the supplied Supreme Court judgment; original lease, administrative record, correspondence, and pleadings were not independently authenticated.
Party claims describe what advocates or litigants asserted; TRUE means the assertion or allegation was recorded, not that the asserted underlying fact is proven.
Legal rules about juridical possession, due process, and holding over are not evidence that the Mimanis continued to occupy the land after requisition.
The first and later High Court orders are separate proceedings: the first used owner and/or occupier language; the second directed owners with independent rights reserved.

The Supreme Court criticized reopening via liberty to mention and certain lower-court observations, yet independently examined entitlement under Article 136; procedural criticism alone does not prove a recipient's right.

The Court did not undertake a fresh determination of the temporary requisition statute's lapse issue and treated proposed reliance on its provisions as unavailable, while construing section 6 only hypothetically.
The record establishes the State's requisition possession, not an actual forcible eviction by the Daw owners and not any completed delivery pursuant to the disputed 1997 notices.

The specific-performance allegation and the pending request to restore that separate suit were not decided on their merits in the supplied judgment; reserved remedies remain subject to independent proceedings.
No inference is drawn from missing witnesses, unknown dates, unshown later proceedings, or unverified identity beyond roles stated in the supplied source.
No premise uses the appeal dismissal or other text labeled DISPOSITION_ONLY as evidence for itself.
